title: How hard is it to find a job in Ireland right now?
excerpt: Unemployment is still low, but more people are competing for each job. Here is what the latest figures mean for jobseekers in Cork and across Ireland.
content_html:
Finding work in Ireland is still possible, but for many jobseekers it takes longer and needs more effort than it did a year or two ago. Here is what the latest figures show, and what they mean for you.

What the official figures say

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) reported that 149,500 people were unemployed in September 2026. The seasonally adjusted rate was 5%, and there were about 5,800 more unemployed people than a year earlier. The overall picture is steady rather than improving quickly.

The rate for people aged 15 to 24 is much higher, at 12.5%. If you are young or starting out, expect more competition for entry-level roles.

What recruiters are seeing

Morgan McKinley's Q3 2026 Ireland employment monitor reports that professional job openings were broadly steady over the quarter, but 4.8% lower than a year earlier. Over the same year, the number of jobseekers rose by 51%. In plain terms, there are fewer openings for each person looking.

Recruiters also describe employers as cautious. Hiring takes longer, and some firms fill business-critical projects with contract staff rather than permanent hires.

What this means for you

  • Apply early. Popular roles can close quickly, so check your job alerts every day.
  • Widen your search. Try related job titles, nearby towns, and temporary or contract work as a way in.
  • Build a steady routine. Ten well-targeted applications each week will do more than forty generic ones.
  • Keep a simple tracker of every application, with the date, the employer, and the contact name. Follow up about a week later.

The short answer

It is harder than it was, mostly because more people are looking for work, not because the jobs have disappeared. Candidates who stand out with a clear, tailored application get the interviews. The next posts in this series cover how to do that, including how to use AI tools safely.

Sources: Central Statistics Office, Monthly Unemployment, September 2026; Morgan McKinley, Ireland Employment Monitor Q3 2026.

title: How to use AI to find jobs online (and stay safe)
excerpt: AI tools can help you tailor your CV, research employers and practise interviews. Here is how to use them well, and how to avoid job scams while you do.
content_html:
AI assistants can save you a lot of time in a job search, as long as you stay in control of what they produce. Here are five practical ways to use them, followed by the safety rules that matter most.

1. Tailor your CV to each job

Paste the job advert and your current CV into an AI assistant and ask it which of your existing skills match the advert's wording. Then make the changes yourself. Check every suggestion, and keep only what is true. An AI tool should never invent experience, qualifications or dates.

2. Research the employer

Ask the assistant to summarise the employer's website, recent news and public reviews, and to suggest three questions to ask at interview. Then check the key facts on the employer's own site, because AI tools can be out of date or simply wrong.

3. Practise interviews

Ask for likely interview questions for the specific role, answer them out loud, and then ask for honest feedback on your answers. Practise with the questions in the advert, since those are the ones the interviewer is most likely to ask.

4. Draft cover notes faster

Give the assistant three points: why you want this job, your two strongest achievements, and the role's main requirements. Edit the draft until it sounds like you. Employers notice generic letters quickly.

5. Set up job alerts

Most major job boards let you save a search and receive email alerts. Set one up for each job title you want, and include a location. Alerts save you from refreshing the same pages every day.

Protect your personal information

Do not paste your PPS number, bank details, date of birth or ID numbers into an AI tool. Only share these through an employer's official application or onboarding process, and only once you are sure the employer is genuine.

Watch for job scams

Scams are common online, and AI has made fake adverts look more convincing. Be cautious if:

  • You are asked to pay for an application, training or equipment before you start work.
  • You are asked for bank details or your PPS number before a proper interview.
  • The job is offered through a messaging app, with no company name or website.
  • You are asked to receive and forward money or parcels for someone else.

If you are unsure, find the employer's website yourself rather than using the link in the message, and phone them directly using the number on their official site.

title: How to stand out from other candidates in Ireland
excerpt: When there are more applicants for each job, a clear and specific application makes the difference. Practical steps for your CV, cover note and interview.
content_html:
When a recruiter has dozens of applications to read, most of them are quickly dismissed. The good news is that a few simple changes can make your application much easier to shortlist.

Start with the job advert

Highlight the five to seven skills the employer asks for. Make sure your CV uses the same words for skills you genuinely have. Recruiters often search CVs for these exact terms.

Show results, not duties

Compare these two lines:

  • Responsible for stock in a busy shop.
  • Managed weekly stock orders for a busy shop, which reduced waste by 15% over six months.

The second line shows what you did and what changed. Only use figures you can back up in an interview.

Make the first page count

Recruiters scan CVs quickly. Put your most relevant experience and skills near the top, keep the CV to two pages, and use one clear font and simple headings. Leave out a photo, date of birth and marital status, which are not normally expected in Ireland.

Prove your skills with certificates

Certificates can move you up a shortlist, especially when they are a requirement. Common examples in Ireland include:

  • Safe Pass, for construction sites
  • Manual handling training, for warehouse, care and retail roles
  • Food safety or food hygiene certificates, for hospitality and food work
  • Driver CPC, for professional drivers
  • Garda vetting, which is needed for some care and childcare roles

Check which certificates the job asks for, and list the ones you have near the top of your CV with their dates.

Write a short, specific cover note

Use three short paragraphs. Say why you want to work for this employer, give one or two concrete examples of what you bring, and explain what you would like to do in the role. Do not repeat your CV word for word.

Prepare for the interview

Research the company, and prepare two or three examples from your experience using the STAR method: the Situation, the Task, the Action you took and the Result. Ask two or three thoughtful questions at the end, such as what a successful first three months looks like.

Follow up

Send a short thank-you email within a day of the interview. If you have not heard back by the date the employer gave, a polite follow-up email is fine. Keep it brief and professional.

title: The Irish CV: format, length and what to leave out
excerpt: Irish employers expect a clear, concise CV. Here is what to include, what to leave out, and how to make it easy to read in under a minute.
content_html:
Irish recruiters usually want a CV that is clear and easy to scan. There is no single required format, but these guidelines will serve you well for most roles.

Length

Two pages is the usual maximum for most jobseekers. Graduates and early-career candidates can often fit everything on one page. Cut anything that is not relevant to the job you are applying for.

What to include

  • Your name and contact details: a mobile number and a professional email address.
  • A short profile of two or three lines, describing the role you want and your strongest skills.
  • Work experience, most recent first, with dates, job titles and achievements.
  • Education and qualifications, including certificates and licences.
  • Relevant skills, such as languages, software or driving licence details.
  • A line on your right to work in Ireland, if it is relevant to the job.

What to leave out

  • A photo, date of birth, marital status or religion. These are not normally expected.
  • References listed by name. Write "References available on request" or simply leave it out.
  • Old or unrelated jobs that take up space. A part-time job from ten years ago does not need detail.
  • Spelling and grammar mistakes. Ask someone else to read the CV before you send it.

Make it easy to read

Use a standard font such as Arial or Calibri at 10 to 12 point, with clear headings and bullet points. Save the file with your name in the title, for example Mary-Murphy-CV.pdf, and send it as a PDF unless the employer asks for a Word file.

Finally, check that the CV matches what you say on LinkedIn and any online application form. Recruiters notice when the details do not agree.

title: Finding work in Cork beyond the job boards
excerpt: Many jobs are filled through networks, local services and direct contact with employers. Here are practical ways to widen your search in Cork.
content_html:
Online job boards are a good starting point, but they are not the only route to work. Many employers fill roles through referrals, local services or by contacting people they already know. Here are some ways to widen your search.

Use the free public employment services

Intreo centres, run by the Department of Social Protection, offer employment support, including help with CVs and interview preparation. The Local Employment Service (LES) also helps people find work in their local area. If you are receiving a jobseeker's payment, your Intreo officer can tell you what support is available.

Check training and apprenticeships

Further education courses and apprenticeships can lead directly to work. SOLAS and the education and training boards publish current courses and apprenticeships, many of them with employers involved. A short certified course can also make you more competitive for the jobs you are targeting.

Speak to employers directly

Choose five employers in Cork that you would like to work for. Visit their websites, look for their careers page, and send a short, polite email to the manager or team lead explaining what you can offer. Many small and medium-sized businesses never advertise their vacancies publicly.

Build your network

Tell friends, family, former colleagues and neighbours what kind of work you are looking for. Ask them to let you know about openings. Keep your LinkedIn profile up to date, and connect with people who work in the sectors you want to enter.

Watch for local events

Job fairs, employer open days and careers talks are often advertised on community boards, local libraries and social media. Attending even one can help you meet people who are hiring.

Keep a steady rhythm

Set aside time each week for your search, including applications, networking and follow-ups. A regular routine is easier to sustain than occasional bursts of effort, and it keeps you moving forward when responses are slow.

title: Which sectors are hiring in Cork right now
excerpt: Hiring is uneven across Cork. Here is how to think about which sectors have steady demand and how to target them.
content_html:
Cork has a broad economy, so job openings come and go by sector. Rather than chase whatever is advertised this week, it helps to know which areas have steady demand over the year.

Sectors with steady demand

  • Healthcare and social care: care assistants, support workers and healthcare assistants are needed all year round.
  • Construction and trades: skills shortages are widely reported, especially for experienced tradespeople and site workers.
  • Logistics and warehousing: stock, picking and driving roles follow consumer demand, which rarely drops to zero.
  • Hospitality and food: cafés, hotels and restaurants hire heavily before busy periods, so openings often appear in waves.

How to use this

Pick two sectors you could work in with a little training. Then read ten adverts in each and note the words that come up again and again. Those repeated words are what employers screen for, so they are the words your CV should use.

Also check which sectors are advertising in your neighbourhood. A role that is 40 minutes away by bus may not be realistic, even if it is perfect on paper.

title: Why job searches take longer in a steady market
excerpt: When the economy is stable rather than booming, employers take more care over hiring. Here is what that means for your search.
content_html:
A steady job market is often better than a booming one for employees, but it can feel slower for jobseekers. Employers are less rushed. They interview more people and take longer to decide.

What you may notice

  • Fewer urgent, same-week vacancies.
  • Longer gaps between the application and the first interview.
  • More rounds of interviews before an offer.

What to do about it

Expect a process of several weeks, and plan your search over months rather than days. Keep applying steadily, so you always have several applications in progress. A search that is paused for a fortnight after one rejection often falls behind.

Use the waiting time well. Improve one part of your application each week, whether that is your CV, your LinkedIn profile or your interview answers.

title: What more jobseekers mean for your application
excerpt: More people are applying for each role than before. Here is how to make your application stand out when competition is high.
content_html:
When more people are looking for work, a recruiter may receive many more applications for the same role. That does not mean you cannot get the job, but it does mean your application has to be easy to shortlist.

Make the match obvious

Recruiters often make a first decision in a few seconds. Make it clear, within the first few lines of your CV and cover letter, that you meet the main requirements of the job.

Apply in a focused way

Ten carefully targeted applications usually produce more interviews than forty generic ones. Choose roles where you already meet most of the requirements, and tailor each application to the advert.

Be easy to contact

Check that your phone number and email address are correct and professional. A missed call from an employer is a missed opportunity.

title: How the Irish job market differs between Dublin and Cork
excerpt: Dublin and Cork have different employers, salaries and commuting realities. Here is how to adjust your search for Cork.
content_html:
Many jobseekers use Dublin job adverts as a guide, but Cork has its own pattern. Its largest employers include multinationals, public bodies, universities, and a strong base of small and medium-sized businesses.

What is different

  • Employer size: many Cork roles are with smaller firms, where one person may cover several tasks.
  • Commuting: travel times are shorter, but public transport can be limited outside the city centre, so check routes before you apply.
  • Networks: local networks matter more in a smaller market. Recommendations and word of mouth can be powerful.

What to do

Search by town as well as by city, including areas such as Carrigaline, Midleton and Mallow if they are within reach. Look at employers that are based locally, not just the ones you have heard of.

title: Hybrid working and what it means for your job search
excerpt: Many employers now mix office and home working. Here is how to ask about it, and how to present your preferences honestly.
content_html:
Hybrid working is common in Ireland, with many roles expecting several days a week in the office. Your preferences matter, but so does being clear about them early.

Find out before you apply

Look for the working pattern in the advert or ask the recruiter. If it is not stated, ask in a friendly way: "Could you tell me what the office attendance expectation is for this role?"

Say what you can do

If you need to work from home on certain days, say so in a calm, practical way. Explain how you will stay available and productive. Employers respond better to a clear plan than to a vague request.

Remember the trade-off

Some employers value in-person teamwork, particularly for new starters. Being willing to attend for training and key meetings can strengthen your application.

title: How to read a job advert for hidden requirements
excerpt: Job adverts say a lot between the lines. Learn to spot what the employer really wants before you apply.
content_html:
A job advert is a short summary of what the employer needs, but the details can tell you more than the title. Learning to read adverts carefully saves time and helps you write a better application.

Look at the order

The first requirement listed is often the most important. Requirements that appear in the job description and again in the person specification are almost certainly essential.

Watch for signals

  • "Fast-paced" often means high volume and tight deadlines.
  • "Self-starter" can mean limited training or supervision.
  • "Team player" usually means the role involves close daily cooperation.
  • "Flexible" may mean shifts, weekends or changing hours.

Respond to all of it

Make sure your CV or cover letter answers each main requirement. If you cannot meet one, be honest about it and show what you bring instead.

title: Temporary and contract work as a way into a permanent job
excerpt: A temporary contract can be a useful first step. Here is how to use it to build experience and get noticed.
content_html:
Temporary and contract work is sometimes seen as second best, but it can be an effective route into a permanent role. Many employers prefer to see a candidate in action before offering a permanent contract.

Make the most of it

  • Arrive early, learn the systems quickly and ask for feedback.
  • Get to know the permanent staff and your manager.
  • Ask whether permanent roles are likely to open, and what you would need to be considered.

Protect your record

Keep a note of what you achieved in each contract. Use this for your CV and in interviews. A reference from a contract manager can be just as valuable as one from a permanent job.

title: Seasonal jobs in Ireland: how to plan your year
excerpt: Many jobs peak at particular times. Here is how to plan your search around seasonal demand in hospitality, retail and tourism.
content_html:
Some jobs are busiest at certain times of year. Hospitality, retail, events and tourism often hire heavily before the summer season and the Christmas period.

When openings tend to appear

  • Late winter and spring: summer staff for hotels, cafés and attractions.
  • Autumn: seasonal retail and warehouse roles for the Christmas period.

How to prepare

Update your CV in advance, so you can apply as soon as adverts appear. Gather references from previous seasonal employers. If you want a year-round role, mention in your application that you are looking for longer-term work, to set expectations.

title: The skills shortage in construction: where the opportunities are
excerpt: Construction firms often struggle to find skilled staff. Here is how to find opportunities, and what employers look for.
content_html:
Construction has reported skills shortages for some time, and many firms are still looking for experienced workers and apprentices. If you work with your hands or want to learn a trade, this is a sector worth researching.

Where to look

  • Main contractors and specialist subcontractors, such as electrical, plumbing and groundworks firms.
  • Local builders and small firms, which often advertise on local boards before larger sites.
  • Apprenticeship programmes through SOLAS, which pair training with paid work.

What employers ask for

A Safe Pass card is required on most sites, so get it early if you do not have it. Full driving licences, reliability and a record of finishing jobs on time all count for a great deal.

title: Healthcare support roles and how to get started
excerpt: Care and healthcare support roles are needed across Ireland. Here is how to get started, and what experience helps.
content_html:
Healthcare support work covers care assistants, healthcare assistants and support workers in residential, community and hospital settings. It is demanding, but it offers steady demand and a chance to build a career.

What helps

  • Experience in caring for family or friends, which you can describe with care and respect.
  • Relevant training, such as manual handling, first aid or dementia awareness.
  • Garda vetting, which many employers need before you start.

What to show in an interview

Employers want patience, reliability and good judgement. Prepare a short example of a time you stayed calm under pressure, and explain how you looked after someone's dignity and comfort.

title: Retail and hospitality hiring: what employers want now
excerpt: Retail and hospitality employers look for reliability and people skills. Here is what to show on your application.
content_html:
Retail and hospitality are among the largest employers of entry-level staff. Competition can be strong for popular roles, so it helps to know what managers look for.

The main qualities

  • Reliability: consistent attendance and punctuality matter more than almost anything else.
  • Customer care: a calm, friendly manner, even on a busy shift.
  • Teamwork: covering for colleagues and sharing tasks.

How to show it

Give examples from any previous role, including volunteering or school work. For example, "I handled busy weekend shifts at a community café and kept our queue moving without rushing customers." Short, specific examples work better than general claims.

title: Warehouse and logistics jobs in Cork: a practical guide
excerpt: Warehouse and logistics roles are common in Cork. Here is what to expect, and how to make your application stronger.
content_html:
Warehouse and logistics work covers picking, packing, stock control, forklift operation and dispatch. It is physically demanding, but it is often a reliable route into work and a stepping stone to supervisor roles.

What employers look for

  • Physical fitness and willingness to work shifts.
  • Accuracy, since small mistakes in stock can be costly.
  • A forklift licence or willingness to train for one.
  • Good timekeeping, especially for early shifts.

Make your application stronger

Mention any stock, inventory or computer system experience, even from a shop job. Explain how you check accuracy, for example by counting and cross-checking orders. These details are exactly what a warehouse manager is looking for.

title: Graduates facing a tougher market: a realistic plan
excerpt: Graduates may find the first job harder to land than they expected. Here is a realistic plan that works, step by step.
content_html:
Many graduates are finding that the first job takes longer than expected. That can be discouraging, but a clear plan makes the process more manageable.

Step 1: Decide what you are aiming for

Choose two or three job titles that match your degree and interests. Being specific makes your applications sharper.

Step 2: Build evidence

Use placements, projects, part-time work and volunteering to show what you can do. Describe what you produced, not just what you studied.

Step 3: Apply and track

Aim for a steady number of applications each week, and track responses. If you are not getting interviews after a month, review your CV before you apply more widely.

Step 4: Keep your options open

A temporary or part-time role in your field can still build experience and contacts while you search.

title: Returning to work after a career break in Ireland
excerpt: A career break for family, health or study is common. Here is how to explain it, and how to rebuild your confidence and CV.
content_html:
Many people return to work after a break. Employers are increasingly used to this, but you do need to explain it clearly and confidently.

Explain the gap simply

You do not need to share personal details. A simple line such as "I took time out to care for family, and I am now looking to return to work" is enough.

Refresh your skills

Consider a short course, a refresher in software you used before, or volunteering. Even a few weeks of current training shows you are ready to work.

Focus on what you bring

Your experience, reliability and judgement have not disappeared. Show how you managed your time, handled responsibility and learned new things during the break.

title: Changing careers in your 40s: where to start
excerpt: A career change at any age is possible. Here is how to decide where to go, and how to present your experience clearly.
content_html:
People change careers in their forties, fifties and beyond. Your experience is an asset, but you need a clear story about why you are moving and where you are going.

Start with the transferable skills

List what you do well: managing people, handling customers, solving problems, meeting deadlines. Many of these skills apply to other sectors.

Test the new field first

Talk to people who work in the area, shadow someone if you can, or take a short course. A test run helps you avoid a costly mistake.

Write a clear story

Your cover letter should explain the move in one or two sentences, then show how your past work prepares you for the new role.

title: Job hopping versus staying: what employers think
excerpt: Frequent job changes can raise questions, but staying too long can also be a concern. Here is how to explain your history.
content_html:
Recruiters often look at how long you stayed in each role. Short stays are not automatically a problem, and long stays are not automatically a strength. What matters is the story behind them.

Explain short stays

If you moved on because a contract ended, the business closed or you took a better opportunity, say so briefly. Focus on what you gained.

Show progress

If you stayed in one place for years, show how your role grew. Promotions, new responsibilities and projects all help.

Be honest

Do not invent reasons. Interviewers often ask follow-up questions, and a clear, honest answer builds trust.

title: Probation periods in Ireland: what to expect
excerpt: Many new jobs include a probation period. Here is what it usually means and how to make the most of it.
content_html:
Many employers include a probation period at the start of a new job. It gives both sides a chance to check that the role is a good fit.

What it usually involves

The probation period is often a few months, with regular reviews. Your employer may set targets or ask you to complete training.

How to make the most of it

  • Ask at the start what success looks like after the probation period.
  • Request feedback at the first review and act on it.
  • Keep a short record of what you have achieved.

Your contract should set out the terms, including notice periods. If anything is unclear, ask your employer or check the official information from the Workplace Relations Commission.

title: Equal treatment in recruitment: what to know
excerpt: Recruitment should be fair and based on your ability to do the job. Here is a general guide to what that means for jobseekers.
content_html:
Irish law protects people from discrimination in employment on a number of grounds, including gender, age, disability, race and family status. This applies to recruitment as well as to working life.

What this means in practice

Employers should base hiring decisions on the skills and experience needed for the role. Questions about family plans, religion or health are generally not appropriate at interview stage.

If something feels wrong

Keep a record of what was said and when. You can find general information on your rights from Citizens Information, and on workplace matters from the Workplace Relations Commission. Getting independent advice is a sensible step if you are unsure.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

title: Minimum wage in Ireland: how to check your pay
excerpt: Knowing the minimum wage helps you judge a job offer. Here is where to check the current rate and what it covers.
content_html:
Ireland has a national minimum wage, which employers must pay to most workers aged 18 and over. It is reviewed from time to time, so always check the current rate before you negotiate.

Where to check

The Workplace Relations Commission and gov.ie publish the current national minimum wage and the rates for younger workers. Check the official website before you accept an offer.

What to look at in an offer

  • The hourly rate, and whether it applies to all hours you work.
  • Any allowances, bonuses or overtime rules.
  • Deductions, such as uniform or training costs.

If an offer falls below the minimum wage, ask the employer to explain, and seek advice if the answer is unsatisfactory.

title: Zero-hour and casual contracts: what to ask before you sign
excerpt: Casual and zero-hour contracts can offer flexibility, but they can also bring uncertainty. Here is what to ask before you agree.
content_html:
Some employers offer contracts with no guaranteed hours. These can suit students and people with changing responsibilities, but they can also make budgeting harder.

Questions to ask

  • What are the typical hours in a normal week, and what is the busiest period?
  • How and when will I be given my rota?
  • What notice do I get if hours are cut?
  • Am I entitled to paid leave, and how is it calculated?

Keep a record

Keep a note of the hours you work each week. This helps if there is a dispute about pay or hours later on.

title: Planning a job search around family life
excerpt: Childcare and family commitments affect when you can work. Here is how to plan a realistic search that fits your life.
content_html:
Finding work around family responsibilities takes planning, but many parents and carers return to work successfully. Being realistic about hours and location is the first step.

Decide your limits

Write down the hours you can work, the days you need off and how far you can travel. This makes it easier to filter adverts and avoid wasted applications.

Look for flexible roles

Part-time, term-time, school-hours and flexible roles are advertised regularly. Use search terms such as "part-time" and "flexible hours" in your job alerts.

Be confident about your needs

You do not need to explain your childcare arrangements in detail. Say clearly what hours you are available for, and why that suits the role.

title: Students looking for part-time work in Cork
excerpt: Part-time work can fund your studies and build useful experience. Here is where to look and how to present your studies.
content_html:
Many students in Cork work part-time alongside their studies. The work can help with money and give you skills employers value, such as time management and teamwork.

Where to look

  • Cafés, restaurants, hotels and retail shops, which often hire students for weekends and evenings.
  • Campus jobs, which can be easier to fit around timetables.
  • Tutoring, customer service and admin roles.

How to present yourself

Mention your course and any relevant projects. Students often underestimate how much they have done, such as group work, presentations or running a society.

title: Remote jobs from Ireland: what to look for
excerpt: Remote roles can open up opportunities, but many are competitive. Here is how to identify genuine remote jobs and apply well.
content_html:
Remote work is attractive, and many people search specifically for it. Before you apply, check that the job is genuinely remote and that the terms suit you.

Check the details

  • Is the role remote from Ireland, or only from a specific country?
  • Does the employer have a registered address and a clear hiring process?
  • Is there a salary range in the advert, and does it match your expectations?

Be careful with scams

Be wary of remote roles that ask you to pay for equipment, buy software or accept money to forward. Check the company on its own website and LinkedIn before you share personal details.

title: Looking for a job while you are still employed
excerpt: Searching for a new role while you have a job takes discipline. Here is how to protect your current position and your privacy.
content_html:
Many people look for a new job while still working. It is sensible, but it needs care so your current role is not affected.

Protect your privacy

Do not use work email or work computers for your search. Be careful about updating your LinkedIn profile, and consider turning on the setting that tells recruiters you are open to work only to those you choose.

Plan interviews carefully

Ask for early or late appointments, or use your annual leave. Be honest with recruiters about your timing, but do not reveal more than you need to.

Keep your current job strong

Continue to do your best work. A strong reference from your current employer is valuable, even if you move on.

title: How to write a CV summary that gets read
excerpt: The summary at the top of your CV is the first thing a recruiter reads. Here is how to write one that makes them keep going.
content_html:
Your CV summary is two to four lines at the top of the page. Its job is to tell the reader who you are and why they should keep reading.

A simple structure

Start with your role or the type of work you do, add your strongest one or two skills, and finish with what you are looking for. For example: "Warehouse operative with four years of stock control and forklift experience. Accurate, reliable and comfortable with inventory software. Seeking a permanent role in logistics in Cork."

What to avoid

  • Vague words like "hard-working" and "passionate" without evidence.
  • Long paragraphs. Keep it short enough to read in five seconds.
  • Repeating your job history. The summary should point forward, not backwards.

Rewrite your summary for each job, using the advert's main skills where they truthfully match yours.

title: CV keywords: matching the advert without copying it
excerpt: Many employers search CVs using keywords. Here is how to include the right terms naturally, without sounding like a template.
content_html:
Many applicant tracking systems and recruiters search for specific words. If your CV does not use the terms in the advert, it may never be seen, even when you are a good match.

Find the keywords

Read the advert and list the skills, tools and qualifications it mentions. Ignore generic words and focus on specific terms such as "stock control", "Microsoft Excel", "food hygiene" or "customer complaints".

Use them honestly

If you have the skill, use the same term in your experience section. If the advert says "stock control" and you did "inventory checks", you can write "inventory checks and stock control" if both are accurate.

Keep it natural

Do not hide keywords in white text or long lists. A short skills section, plus keywords woven into your achievements, reads well to both machines and people.

title: Writing a CV with no work experience
excerpt: No experience is not the same as no skills. Here is how to build a strong first CV using school, volunteering and everyday responsibilities.
content_html:
If you are leaving school, returning to the workforce or applying for your first job, your CV may feel empty. In practice, most people have more to show than they think.

Where to find evidence

  • School or college projects, presentations and group work.
  • Volunteering, such as sports coaching, community events or charity shops.
  • Family responsibilities, such as managing a household budget or caring for relatives.
  • Hobbies that involved organising, teaching or leading others.

How to present it

Use a heading such as "Relevant experience" or "Projects and volunteering". Describe what you did and what you learned. For example: "Organised a sponsored run for 120 people, managing a budget of 800 euro and a team of six volunteers."

title: How to present gaps in your CV honestly
excerpt: Gaps in your work history are common. Here is how to show them clearly without drawing unnecessary attention.
content_html:
Gaps in a CV are normal. Recruiters are more concerned by vague or confusing timelines than by a known break in work.

Keep dates consistent

Show months and years for each role, so the timeline is easy to follow. Do not hide gaps by listing only years, as this can look evasive.

Use a short line when needed

You can add a line such as "Career break for family caring, 2023 to 2025" or "Full-time study, 2022 to 2024". Briefly mention any courses, volunteering or freelance work you did during the period.

Be ready to talk about it

Prepare a one or two sentence answer for interview. Explain what you did during the break, why you are ready to return and what you bring now. Then move the conversation back to the job.

title: CV skills section: what counts and what doesn't
excerpt: A skills section can help a recruiter find what they need quickly. Here is how to choose the right skills to list.
content_html:
A skills section is useful when it is specific and honest. A long list of generic words adds little, and an unsupported claim can be found out in interview.

Good skills to list

  • Named software, such as Microsoft Excel, Word, Sage or a specific booking system.
  • Licences and certificates, such as a driving licence, Safe Pass or food hygiene training.
  • Languages, with a clear level, such as "Fluent in Polish" or "Conversational Spanish".

Skills that need evidence

Words such as "communication" or "teamwork" are better shown in your experience section than listed alone. Make sure every skill you list could be discussed in an interview.

Keep it short

Six to ten items is usually enough. Put the most relevant ones first, and change the list for each job.

title: Writing achievements when your job was just a job
excerpt: You do not need a high-flying title to show achievements. Here is how to describe everyday work in ways that stand out.
content_html:
Many people undersell their work because it feels routine. But routine work often includes problems solved, standards kept and people helped.

Ask three questions

  • What did I do better than the standard expectation?
  • What problem did I notice and fix?
  • What did I train, help or improve?

Add numbers where you can

For example: "Served an average of 150 customers per shift" or "Checked deliveries of over 300 items a day with a 99% accuracy rate." Only use numbers you can explain.

Keep the language plain

Employers do not need fancy words. Clear, specific statements read better than jargon.

title: How long should a cover letter be in Ireland
excerpt: A cover letter should be short enough to read quickly and long enough to add something new to your CV. Here is a practical guide.
content_html:
Most cover letters in Ireland work best at around one page, usually three or four short paragraphs. Recruiters may read dozens in a day, so brevity matters.

What each paragraph does

  • Opening: the role you are applying for and why it interests you.
  • Middle: one or two examples that match the job's main requirements.
  • Closing: what you would like to do next, such as an interview.

What to avoid

Do not repeat your CV line by line. The cover letter should explain, not list. If the advert does not ask for a cover letter, a short paragraph in the application box may be enough.

title: Cover letter opening lines that work
excerpt: The first sentence of your cover letter decides whether the reader continues. Here are approaches that work well.
content_html:
Many cover letters start with "I am writing to apply for...". That is not wrong, but it does not stand out. A strong opening shows interest and relevance straight away.

Three approaches

  • Link to the employer: "I have shopped at your Cork store for years, and I would like to help the team that makes it run."
  • Lead with your best match: "With four years of stock control experience, I believe I can help your warehouse reduce delivery errors."
  • Explain your reason: "After working in childcare for six years, I want to build my career in primary school support."

Choose the approach that fits you, and keep the sentence specific and honest.

title: Cover letter closing and call to action
excerpt: Your closing paragraph should make it easy for the employer to take the next step. Here is how to write one.
content_html:
The last paragraph of a cover letter is often the most overlooked. A clear closing tells the reader what you want, and makes it easy to reply.

A simple closing

"Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome the chance to discuss how my experience in stock control could help your team. I am available for interview at any time that suits you."

Tips

  • Thank the reader for their time.
  • State that you would welcome an interview or a conversation.
  • Make sure your contact details are visible.

Keep it polite and confident, without sounding pushy.

title: Cover letter for a job you are underqualified for
excerpt: Sometimes the role is a stretch. Here is how to write a cover letter that is honest about your gaps and still persuasive.
content_html:
You do not always need to meet every requirement to apply for a job. Many employers hire people who are close, especially when the candidate learns quickly and brings something valuable.

Lead with your strengths

Start with the requirements you do meet, and give evidence for each one.

Address the gap directly

If a key requirement is missing, say so briefly and show what you are doing about it, such as a course you have started or relevant experience that is close. For example: "I have not yet used Sage, but I completed an online course last month and I learn new software quickly."

Be honest

Do not claim skills you do not have. Interviewers often test them, and honesty builds more trust than an overstatement.

title: Writing a CV for a career change
excerpt: Changing careers means your CV has to tell a new story. Here is how to highlight what transfers and reduce what does not.
content_html:
When you move to a different field, recruiters may not immediately see the connection. Your CV should make it clear in seconds.

Lead with the transferable skills

Use your profile and skills section to name the abilities that matter in the new role, such as customer care, project planning or working with data.

Reorder your experience

Put the most relevant experience first, even if it is not your most recent job. You can shorten older roles that are less relevant.

Add evidence from the new field

Courses, volunteering, personal projects and small freelance tasks all show commitment. List them clearly with dates.

title: CV layouts: one column versus two columns
excerpt: The layout of your CV affects how easy it is to read. Here is why a simple one-column design usually works best.
content_html:
CV designs can be creative, but the most important thing is readability. Recruiters and software need to read your information in the right order.

Why one column usually wins

  • It reads in a clear, top-to-bottom order.
  • It works better with applicant tracking systems.
  • It prints and displays well on any device.

When two columns can work

Some creative roles accept more design. Even then, keep the main content simple and make sure the text can be copied and read by software.

Practical tips

Use clear headings, consistent spacing and a readable font. Avoid tables, text boxes and images for your key information.

title: Using a CV template safely
excerpt: Templates can save time, but they can also make your CV look generic. Here is how to use one without losing your personality.
content_html:
A good template gives you structure and saves time. The risk is that many people use the same one, and your CV ends up looking like everyone else's.

Keep the structure, change the content

Use the template for layout, but write your own summary, achievements and skills. Replace any sample text completely.

Check for problems

  • Text that is hard to copy, such as text inside images.
  • Headers and footers that may not be read by software.
  • Icons or graphics that distract from your information.

Before you send, copy all the text from your CV into a plain text file. If the content looks jumbled, simplify the design.

title: Proofreading your CV: a checklist
excerpt: Small mistakes can cost you an interview. Use this checklist to check your CV before you send it.
content_html:
Recruiters notice spelling, dates and formatting errors quickly. A careful final check takes 15 minutes and can make a real difference.

Checklist

  • Check the employer's name and the job title in your cover letter.
  • Check your name, phone number and email address.
  • Read every line aloud, to catch missing words.
  • Check dates for each role and qualification.
  • Use the same tense for past and current roles consistently.
  • Look for repeated words and weak phrases.

Ask a friend to read it as well. A fresh pair of eyes often finds mistakes you have stopped seeing.

title: Saving your CV as a PDF and naming it well
excerpt: A clear file name and the right format make your CV easy to open and easy to find. Here is how to do it.
content_html:
It may seem minor, but how you save your CV matters. A file called "final_v3_new.docx" looks less professional than one with a clear name.

Naming

Use your name and the word CV, for example "Sean-Kelly-CV.pdf". If you are applying for a specific job, you can add the job title, but keep it short.

Format

Send a PDF unless the employer asks for a Word file. A PDF keeps your layout, but check that the text can still be selected, so software can read it.

Size

Keep the file small, ideally under 2 MB. Large files may be blocked by email systems.

title: Online application forms: how to answer without rewriting your CV
excerpt: Many employers use online forms that ask the same questions as your CV. Here is how to answer them quickly and consistently.
content_html:
Online application forms can be tedious, especially when they ask for your work history again. The trick is to prepare a master document you can copy from.

Prepare a master document

Keep a file with your job titles, dates, responsibilities, achievements, references and common answers. Copy from it into each form, and adjust the wording for the role.

Be consistent

Use the same dates and job titles as your CV. Mismatches can slow down the recruiter and raise questions.

Save a copy

Many forms do not save your answers if you leave the page. Write longer answers in a document first, then paste them in.

title: Motivation statements for application forms
excerpt: Some forms ask why you want the job. Here is how to write a short answer that feels genuine and specific.
content_html:
"Why do you want to work for us?" is a common question on application forms. Vague answers are easy to spot, so aim for something specific and honest.

Three parts

  • What attracts you to the employer, such as their work, values or reputation.
  • Why this role fits your skills and goals.
  • What you hope to contribute.

Example

"I am drawn to your work supporting local families, and I would like to build my career in community services. My experience in customer care and volunteering would help me support clients with respect and patience."

Keep your answer to the word limit, and avoid copying the job description word for word.

title: How to write about your salary expectations
excerpt: Salary questions can feel uncomfortable. Here is how to answer them clearly, without undervaluing yourself.
content_html:
Many applications ask about your salary expectations. It is a fair question, and a considered answer helps both sides.

Research first

Check similar roles in Cork on job boards, and look at published pay ranges where they exist. Consider your experience and the responsibilities of the role.

Give a range

A range is often more practical than a single figure. For example: "I am looking for a salary in the range of 32,000 to 35,000 euro, depending on the full package and responsibilities."

Stay flexible

If the advert shows a pay range, you can refer to it. If you prefer to discuss salary later, say so politely: "I would be happy to discuss pay once I understand the full scope of the role."

title: CV references: who to ask and how to ask
excerpt: A good reference can help you get the job. Here is how to choose referees and ask them in a way that works for everyone.
content_html:
References are often requested after an interview, but it helps to prepare them in advance. A reference who knows your work well is more useful than a famous name.

Choose the right people

  • A recent manager or supervisor who saw your work.
  • A colleague or teacher who can speak to your skills.
  • Someone who will respond promptly and speak positively.

Ask politely

Ask first, rather than assuming. Explain the role you are applying for and what you would like them to highlight. Give them a copy of your CV so they can speak accurately.

Thank them

Let your referees know the outcome, whatever it is. It keeps the relationship strong for the future.

title: Volunteering on your CV
excerpt: Volunteer work shows commitment and skills. Here is how to include it so it adds real value to your application.
content_html:
Volunteering is valuable, and many employers recognise it as real experience. The key is to describe what you did in a way that relates to the job.

Give it a clear heading

Use a heading such as "Volunteering" or "Community involvement", and include the organisation, your role and the dates.

Describe the impact

For example: "Coordinated a team of eight volunteers at a food bank, handling weekly stock lists and rotas." This shows organisation, teamwork and reliability.

Choose what to show

You do not need to list every volunteer role. Pick the ones that match the job or show skills employers want.

title: Languages on your CV: how to show your level
excerpt: Language skills are valuable in Ireland's diverse workplaces. Here is how to show your level clearly and honestly.
content_html:
Many employers in Cork value candidates who speak more than one language, whether for customer service, healthcare or international business. The challenge is describing your level accurately.

Use plain descriptions

  • Native: your first language.
  • Fluent: you can work comfortably in it all day.
  • Conversational: you can hold everyday conversations confidently.
  • Basic: you can handle simple phrases and questions.

Give evidence

If you use a language at work or in volunteering, say so. "Used Polish daily to assist customers in a retail store" is more convincing than a level alone.

title: Updating your CV every six months
excerpt: Keeping your CV up to date saves stress when an opportunity appears. Here is a simple routine to follow.
content_html:
Many people only update their CV when they need a job. That makes the process harder, because details are forgotten and deadlines are tight.

A simple routine

Every six months, add your recent work, courses and achievements while they are fresh. Note any new software, licences or responsibilities. Remove anything no longer relevant.

Keep a running log

Create a document where you add one or two lines each month about what you did. When you need your CV, you will have plenty of material to choose from.

Check your details

Review your phone number, email address and any links, such as LinkedIn, to make sure they are current.

title: Writing a short bio for a job application
excerpt: Some applications ask for a short biography. Here is how to write one that sums you up in a few clear sentences.
content_html:
A short bio, often around 50 to 100 words, is used in applications, conference programmes and internal updates. It needs to be clear and warm, but not too personal.

Structure

Start with your current role or the type of work you do. Add a sentence on your experience and key strengths, then one on what you are looking for next.

Example

"I am a support worker with five years of experience in residential care. I enjoy building trust with people and working closely with families. I am now looking for a role that lets me develop my skills in person-centred care."

Write a few versions and choose the one that sounds most like you.

title: Common CV mistakes that cost interviews
excerpt: A few simple errors can stop a strong candidate from getting an interview. Here are the most common ones to avoid.
content_html:
Most CV mistakes are easy to fix, but they can be costly. Recruiters often make quick decisions, so small problems matter.

The most common mistakes

  • Spelling errors, particularly in the employer's name.
  • No clear job title or summary, so the reader cannot see the match.
  • Duties listed without any results.
  • Unprofessional email addresses.
  • Photos, personal details or unrelated hobbies taking up space.
  • The same CV sent to every employer.

Fix these first, then focus on making each achievement specific.

title: What to do first after an interview invitation
excerpt: You have been invited to interview. Here is a simple plan for the next few days to prepare well.
content_html:
An interview invitation is good news, and it is worth treating it as a project with a few clear steps.

Confirm the details

Check the date, time, format and location, and who you will meet. Reply promptly to confirm, and ask about anything you do not know.

Research the employer

Read the company's website, recent news and the job description. Note two or three things that interest you about the employer.

Prepare your examples

Choose three or four examples from your experience that match the job's main requirements. Practise explaining them out loud, in about two minutes each.

Plan the logistics

Know your route, allow extra time and have your ID and documents ready. For video interviews, test your equipment the day before.

title: Phone interviews: how to prepare
excerpt: A phone interview is often the first screening step. Here is how to prepare so you sound confident and clear.
content_html:
Phone interviews are common for early screening. Without body language to help, your voice and clear answers do most of the work.

Set up properly

  • Choose a quiet room with a good signal.
  • Keep your CV, the job advert and your notes in front of you.
  • Have water nearby, and stand or sit upright, which helps your voice sound steady.

Prepare short answers

Phone screens are usually short. Practise answers of 60 to 90 seconds that cover your experience, why you want the role and your availability.

Ask questions

Prepare two or three questions about the role, the team and the next steps.

title: Video interviews: a setup checklist
excerpt: Video interviews are now routine. Here is a checklist to make sure the technology does not get in the way.
content_html:
A video interview is a real interview, and small technical problems can distract from your answers. A little preparation helps you focus on the conversation.

Checklist

  • Test your camera, microphone and internet connection the day before.
  • Choose a quiet room with a plain background and good light in front of you.
  • Close other apps and turn off notifications.
  • Log in five minutes early, with the link ready.
  • Have your CV and notes nearby, but avoid reading from them.

Look at the camera

Eye contact on video means looking at the camera rather than the screen. It feels odd at first, but it makes you appear more engaged.

title: Answering 'Tell me about yourself'
excerpt: This is often the first question, and it sets the tone. Here is how to answer it in about a minute.
content_html:
"Tell me about yourself" is not an invitation to share your life story. It is a chance to give a short professional summary that leads into the rest of the interview.

A simple structure

  • Present: your current role or the type of work you do.
  • Past: one or two key experiences that prepare you for this job.
  • Future: why this role interests you now.

Example

"I am a warehouse supervisor with six years in stock control. I have led teams of up to eight people and reduced stock discrepancies in my last role. I am looking for a role where I can develop my leadership in a larger operation, which is why this position appealed to me."

title: Answering 'Why do you want to work here?'
excerpt: This question tests your research and motivation. Here is how to give a specific, sincere answer.
content_html:
Interviewers ask this to see whether you have thought about the employer, not just the job. A generic answer suggests you are applying everywhere.

Research first

Find two or three things that matter to you about the employer, such as its services, its community involvement or its approach to training.

Link it to yourself

Connect the employer's work to your skills and goals. For example: "I have been a customer of your Cork branch for years, and I like how your team takes time with each person. I want to bring that same care to my work."

Keep it short

Aim for 30 to 45 seconds. Then invite a follow-up question.

title: Answering 'What are your weaknesses?'
excerpt: This question can feel like a trap. Here is how to answer honestly while showing that you are working on it.
content_html:
Interviewers want to see self-awareness. The best answer names a real weakness that is not critical to the role, and shows what you are doing about it.

A useful formula

Name the weakness, explain how it affects you, and describe the steps you are taking. For example: "I sometimes take on too much at once, so I now write a daily priority list and check it with my manager."

Avoid

  • Clichés, such as "I work too hard" or "I am a perfectionist" presented as strengths.
  • Weaknesses that are central to the job, such as poor attention to detail for an accounts role.

title: The STAR method with examples
excerpt: STAR helps you give clear, structured answers to competency questions. Here is how to use it with real examples.
content_html:
STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action and Result. It keeps your answers focused and gives the interviewer what they need to assess you.

The four parts

  • Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences.
  • Task: what you needed to achieve.
  • Action: what you did, in specific steps.
  • Result: what happened, ideally with a measure.

Example

Question: "Tell me about a time you dealt with an unhappy customer."

Answer: "In my café job, a customer's order was wrong during a busy lunch rush. I apologised, remade the order immediately and offered a drink on the house. The customer left a thank-you note, and our manager asked me to train new staff on handling complaints."

title: Handling questions you cannot answer
excerpt: Sometimes an interviewer asks something you do not know. Here is how to respond calmly and still show your ability.
content_html:
No candidate knows everything. How you handle a gap in your knowledge is often more revealing than the answer itself.

What to do

  • Pause briefly and think, rather than rushing.
  • Say honestly what you do not know, and explain how you would find out.
  • Link to a related experience if you have one.

For example: "I have not used that exact system, but I have used a similar one. I learn new software quickly, and I would expect to be productive within a few weeks."

Never make up an answer. Interviewers often ask follow-up questions.

title: Asking good questions at the end of an interview
excerpt: The questions you ask show how much you have thought about the job. Here is how to choose strong ones.
content_html:
Almost every interview ends with "Do you have any questions for us?" Having two or three prepared questions shows that you are interested and thoughtful.

Good questions

  • What does success look like in this role after six months?
  • What are the biggest challenges the team is facing right now?
  • How would you describe the team culture?
  • What are the next steps in the process?

Avoid

Avoid asking about pay, holidays or leaving early at this stage, unless the interviewer raises them. Save those questions for a later offer conversation.

title: Dressing for interviews in Ireland
excerpt: Dress codes vary, but being neat and appropriate matters. Here is a practical guide for most interviews in Ireland.
content_html:
The right outfit depends on the employer. A corporate office, a café and a construction site have very different norms. The safest rule is to dress one step above the normal daily dress for that workplace.

General guidance

  • Clean, ironed clothes that fit well.
  • Simple colours and minimal jewellery.
  • Comfortable shoes, polished if they are formal.
  • Good personal hygiene and neat hair.

Check the workplace

If you are unsure, ask the recruiter what is typical. Visit the workplace or look at staff photos online to get a sense of the culture.

title: Interview nerves: practical ways to stay calm
excerpt: Nerves are normal before an interview. Here are simple techniques that help you feel steadier and think clearly.
content_html:
Feeling nervous shows that you care about the outcome. The goal is not to remove nerves entirely, but to keep them from taking over.

Before the interview

  • Prepare well, so you feel ready rather than hopeful.
  • Plan your journey and arrive early, but not too early.
  • Practise slow breathing: in for four counts, out for six.

During the interview

If your mind goes blank, pause, take a breath and ask the interviewer to repeat the question. Speaking more slowly than you think you should often helps.

After the interview

Note what went well and what you would change. Every interview is practice for the next one.

title: Competency-based interviews explained
excerpt: Many Irish employers use competency questions to assess your skills. Here is what they are and how to prepare.
content_html:
Competency-based interviews ask about past behaviour to predict future performance. Questions often start with "Tell me about a time when..." or "Give me an example of...".

Common competencies

  • Teamwork and collaboration
  • Communication and influencing
  • Problem solving and decision making
  • Customer focus
  • Handling pressure and deadlines

How to prepare

Read the job advert and match each requirement to a competency. Prepare one STAR example for each, and check that it shows what you did rather than what the team did.

title: Panel interviews: how to handle several interviewers
excerpt: A panel interview means answering several people at once. Here is how to keep your focus and build rapport with everyone.
content_html:
Panel interviews can feel intimidating, but they are a normal part of hiring, especially for senior or public-sector roles.

Before

Ask who will be on the panel and what their roles are. Research each person briefly on LinkedIn or the company site.

During

  • Make eye contact with the person who asked the question, then include the rest of the panel.
  • Take a moment to note names, so you can address people directly.
  • Keep your answers focused. Several interviewers mean less time for each question.

After

Send a thank-you email to the panel, or to the main contact, within a day.

title: Group interviews and assessment days
excerpt: Some employers assess candidates in groups. Here is how to show your strengths without dominating the group.
content_html:
Group interviews and assessment days often include a group task, a short presentation or a discussion. Employers are looking at how you contribute, not just what you say.

What works

  • Listen carefully, and build on what others say.
  • Invite quieter people into the discussion.
  • Offer a clear suggestion, and summarise the group's progress when it helps.

What to avoid

Do not interrupt others or try to take control of every decision. A team player who helps the group reach a good result is more memorable than the loudest voice in the room.

title: Technical tests and practical assessments
excerpt: Some jobs include a skills test. Here is how to prepare for practical assessments in office, trade and care roles.
content_html:
Practical tests are common for roles that depend on specific skills, such as typing, spreadsheets, driving, trades or care tasks. The best preparation is to practise the skill itself.

Before the test

  • Ask what the test covers and how long it lasts.
  • Check whether you need any equipment or documents.
  • Practise under time pressure if the test is timed.

During the test

Read the instructions carefully, work steadily and ask a question if something is unclear. Accuracy usually matters more than speed, unless the role is explicitly about speed.

title: Salary questions in interviews
excerpt: You may be asked about your salary expectations during an interview. Here is how to answer with confidence.
content_html:
Salary questions can feel like a test, but they are a normal part of the process. A calm, prepared answer helps you avoid undervaluing yourself.

Prepare before the interview

Research pay for similar roles in Cork, and decide on a realistic range based on your experience and the responsibilities of the job.

Answer clearly

"Based on my research and experience, I am looking for a salary in the range of 34,000 to 37,000 euro. I am open to discussing the full package." Then stop talking and let the interviewer respond.

If the range is lower

Ask about the total package, including training, hours and benefits, before you decide.

title: Following up after an interview
excerpt: A short, polite follow-up after an interview shows interest and keeps you on the employer's radar. Here is how.
content_html:
Following up is expected in most hiring processes. A brief, well-written message is professional, and it can help you stand out.

The thank-you email

Send it within 24 hours. Thank the interviewer, mention one specific point from the conversation and restate your interest.

Example

"Thank you for meeting me today. I enjoyed learning about the new stock system, and I am keen to help the team reduce delivery errors. Please let me know if you need anything else from me."

If you hear nothing

If the employer gave a date for a decision, wait until the day after. Then send one polite follow-up asking for an update.

title: What to do after a rejection
excerpt: A rejection is disappointing, but it is also useful information. Here is how to respond and learn from it.
content_html:
Rejection is a normal part of job searching, even for strong candidates. How you respond can affect future opportunities.

Respond politely

Reply with a short thank-you message. Ask, if you wish, for brief feedback on your interview. Many employers will not reply, but some will.

Review honestly

Note what you were asked, what you answered well and what you would change. Look for patterns across several interviews rather than focusing on one.

Keep going

Use what you learned to improve your next application. Most successful candidates were rejected several times before they got the job they wanted.

title: Second interviews: what changes
excerpt: A second interview usually goes deeper. Here is how to prepare for the extra questions and the decision-makers.
content_html:
Reaching a second interview is a strong sign. It usually means you have passed the first screen, and the employer wants to test your fit more closely.

What is different

  • You may meet a senior manager or a future colleague.
  • Questions may be more detailed or technical.
  • You may be asked about your plans, your salary or your start date.

How to prepare

Review your notes from the first interview. Prepare thoughtful questions for the new interviewer, and think about how you would tackle the first few months in the role.

title: Interview body language
excerpt: Your body language affects how interviewers see you. Here are simple habits that make a good impression.
content_html:
Body language is not about performing. It is about showing that you are engaged, calm and open to the conversation.

Helpful habits

  • Sit upright and lean in slightly to show interest.
  • Make eye contact, but do not stare.
  • Use a firm, brief handshake if the setting is in person.
  • Rest your hands on the table or in your lap, not fidgeting.

Practise

Record a short practice answer on your phone and watch it back. Most people notice habits they did not know they had.

title: Interviewing when English is your second language
excerpt: Being fluent but not a native speaker can feel challenging. Here is how to prepare and show your strengths clearly.
content_html:
Many people interview in English when it is not their first language. Employers value the skills and experience you bring, and most recruiters are used to working with diverse teams.

Prepare your key messages

Know your main points in advance, and practise saying them clearly. Short sentences are easier to follow.

Ask for clarity

If you do not understand a question, ask politely: "Could you rephrase that?" This is better than guessing.

Show your strengths

Your ability to work across languages and cultures is valuable in many workplaces. Mention it where it is relevant, such as customer service or international teams.

title: Recovering from a bad interview
excerpt: Every candidate has an interview that does not go well. Here is how to move on and make the next one better.
content_html:
You may leave an interview feeling you did not perform well. It happens to everyone. What matters is what you do next.

Take a short break

Allow yourself a little time to reset, then review the interview calmly.

Identify one or two lessons

Did you run out of time, struggle with one question or forget a key point? Choose one practical change for next time, rather than criticising yourself overall.

Prepare again

Practise the questions that caused difficulty, using your notes. Confidence grows with practice, and each interview helps.

title: Interviews for entry-level jobs
excerpt: Entry-level interviews focus on attitude and potential more than experience. Here is what employers are usually looking for.
content_html:
When you have little work experience, interviewers focus on your reliability, willingness to learn and attitude towards customers or colleagues.

What to show

  • Enthusiasm for the role and the employer.
  • Examples from school, volunteering or family life that show responsibility.
  • Your availability and reliability, stated clearly.

Common questions

You may be asked why you want the job, how you handle busy periods or what you would do if you made a mistake. Prepare honest, simple answers that show your judgement.

title: Interviews for management roles
excerpt: Management interviews test leadership, decision-making and how you develop others. Here is how to prepare.
content_html:
Management interviews look beyond your own work. Employers want to know how you lead teams, handle difficult conversations and deliver results.

Prepare examples of leadership

Choose examples where you led a team through change, improved a process, coached a colleague or managed a poor performance situation fairly.

Show your approach

Explain how you set goals, communicate expectations and measure progress. Interviewers are often testing your style as much as your results.

Ask about the team

Ask about current challenges and what the team needs from its next manager. This shows you are thinking like a leader.

title: Preparing a 60-second introduction
excerpt: A short introduction can help at networking events, interviews and job fairs. Here is how to write and practise one.
content_html:
A 60-second introduction is a short, clear summary of who you are and what you are looking for. It is useful in many situations, from a job fair stand to a first meeting with a manager.

Structure

  • Your name and what you do.
  • One or two strengths or achievements.
  • What you are looking for next.

Example

"Hi, I am Aoife. I work in customer service, and I am known for calm, clear communication with difficult customers. I am looking for a role in a team where I can build on my skills in training new staff."

Practise it until it sounds natural, not memorised.

title: How to make a proper LinkedIn profile
excerpt: A complete LinkedIn profile helps recruiters find you and understand you quickly. Here is a step-by-step guide.
content_html:
LinkedIn is where many recruiters start their search. A complete, clear profile makes it far more likely that you will be found and contacted.

Step by step

  1. Photo: a clear, recent headshot against a plain background.
  2. Headline: a short line that names your role and strengths.
  3. About: a short summary of your experience and what you want next.
  4. Experience: your roles, with achievements rather than duties.
  5. Skills: ten or more relevant skills, pinned to the top.
  6. Location and contact: your area and how you prefer to be contacted.

Aim for a profile that matches your CV. Mismatched details make recruiters doubt both documents.

title: LinkedIn headline: what to write
excerpt: The headline is the line under your name, and it is one of the most important parts of your profile. Here is how to write a good one.
content_html:
Your LinkedIn headline appears in search results and next to your name in messages. It is a short advert for you, so make it count.

Include your role and strengths

Instead of "Job seeker", try "Warehouse supervisor | Stock control and team leadership | Cork". This tells the reader what you do and what you are good at.

Use keywords

Include the job titles and skills that recruiters search for in your sector. Keep it honest and readable.

Keep it short

LinkedIn shows a limited number of characters in many views. Put the most important words first.

title: LinkedIn About section: a template structure
excerpt: The About section tells your story in a few paragraphs. Here is a simple structure you can adapt.
content_html:
The About section is where you explain who you are in more depth. It should be easy to read, specific and written in your own voice.

A simple structure

  • Opening: who you are and the work you do.
  • Experience: two or three achievements, with results where possible.
  • Skills: the main strengths you bring.
  • Next step: the kind of role or project you are looking for, and how people can contact you.

Example opening

"I help small teams keep their stock accurate and their deliveries on time. Over the past six years in Cork warehouses, I have cut stock discrepancies by a fifth and trained more than twenty new staff."

title: LinkedIn photo and banner basics
excerpt: Your photo and banner are the first visual impression on LinkedIn. Here is how to choose them well.
content_html:
Profiles with a photo tend to attract more interest, so it is worth getting one that looks professional and approachable.

Photo tips

  • Use a recent photo of just you, facing the camera.
  • Choose a plain or softly blurred background.
  • Smile naturally and keep your face well lit.
  • Dress as you would for the kind of job you want.

Banner

The banner is optional. If you use one, keep it simple: a clean image, your sector, or a short line about what you do. Avoid busy graphics that distract from your profile.

title: Adding skills and endorsements on LinkedIn
excerpt: Skills and endorsements can help recruiters find you through searches. Here is how to use them well.
content_html:
The skills section on LinkedIn is searchable, so the right skills can bring you to the attention of recruiters who are looking for them.

Choose relevant skills

List skills that appear in the job adverts you want. Put the most important ones first, and remove skills that do not support your goals.

Endorsements

Endorsements from colleagues add credibility, but they are only useful if they support what you actually do. You can ask people you have worked with to endorse specific skills.

Keep it current

Review your skills every few months and add any new training or software you have learned.

title: Asking for LinkedIn recommendations
excerpt: A short recommendation from someone you have worked with can add real credibility. Here is how to ask for one.
content_html:
Recommendations on LinkedIn are written testimonials. A specific, honest recommendation from a manager or colleague can help a recruiter trust your work.

Who to ask

Choose people who have seen your work directly, such as a former manager, a team lead or a client. Avoid asking people who cannot speak to your skills.

How to ask

Send a personal message, explain what you would value them highlighting, and offer to write a draft they can edit. Most people are happy to help when the request is clear.

Say thank you

Thank them when the recommendation is published, and keep the relationship active.

title: How to apply for jobs on LinkedIn: Easy Apply versus the company site
excerpt: LinkedIn offers Easy Apply and links to company websites. Here is how each works, and when to use which.
content_html:
On LinkedIn you may see two kinds of application. Easy Apply uses your LinkedIn profile to send an application quickly. Other adverts send you to the employer's own site.

Easy Apply

Good for speed, especially when you have many matches. Make sure your profile, phone number and email address are correct, because they are sent automatically. You can usually add a CV and a short message.

Company website

Often gives you a fuller application with forms and more detail. If a job asks you to apply on the company site, do that, even if Easy Apply is available.

A practical rule

For roles you really want, apply through the company site where possible, and add a personal message to the recruiter if you can find one.

title: Applying for jobs on LinkedIn: a step-by-step plan
excerpt: A simple routine for searching and applying on LinkedIn each week. Here is a plan you can follow without losing hours.
content_html:
LinkedIn is useful for finding jobs, but it is easy to spend hours scrolling. A short, regular plan keeps your search focused.

Weekly plan

  1. Set up job alerts for your target titles and locations.
  2. Review new alerts twice a week and save the best matches.
  3. Research each employer briefly, including recent posts and staff profiles.
  4. Apply to the most suitable roles, tailoring your CV or cover note.
  5. Send a short note to one recruiter or hiring manager per application if you can find them.

Track each application in a simple spreadsheet, so you know what to follow up on.

title: LinkedIn job alerts: set them up properly
excerpt: Job alerts save time and bring new roles to you. Here is how to set them up so they are useful, not noisy.
content_html:
Job alerts send you email or app notifications when new jobs match your search. Used well, they keep you informed. Used badly, they fill your inbox.

Set them up well

  • Use specific job titles, such as "Customer service supervisor" rather than "Manager".
  • Choose a sensible location and distance.
  • Set the frequency to daily or weekly, depending on how active you are.

Review regularly

Update your alerts every month. Remove titles that do not bring results, and add new ones as your goals change.

title: Using LinkedIn to research a company before you apply
