excerpt: LinkedIn can tell you a lot about an employer before you apply. Here is what to look at and how to use it wisely.
content_html:
Before you apply or attend an interview, LinkedIn is a useful source of information about the organisation and the people in it.

What to check

  • The company page: size, location, industry and recent updates.
  • Employees: check who works there, and whether any of them share your background or interests.
  • Posts: see what the company talks about and how it presents itself.

Use it with care

Do not contact employees to ask for a job. Instead, read their public posts, and use what you learn to tailor your application and interview answers.

title: Connecting with recruiters on LinkedIn
excerpt: Recruiters are often the gatekeepers to interesting jobs. Here is how to connect with them professionally.
content_html:
Many recruiters in Ireland use LinkedIn to find candidates. Building a professional connection can help you hear about roles early.

Find the right recruiters

Search for recruiters who work in your sector or location. Look at who has posted jobs you have applied for, and at the company's recruiters listed on their page.

Send a clear request

Add a short note, such as: "I am a warehouse supervisor in Cork, and I would welcome the chance to stay in touch about suitable roles."

Keep it respectful

Do not send repeated messages, and reply promptly if a recruiter contacts you. Good communication builds lasting professional relationships.

title: Posting on LinkedIn without feeling awkward
excerpt: Posting can help you be seen, even when you are job searching. Here is how to share useful content without oversharing.
content_html:
Many jobseekers feel uncomfortable posting online. But thoughtful posts about your work and interests can help recruiters and contacts understand what you care about.

Easy things to share

  • A short reflection on something you learned at work or in training.
  • A useful article from your sector, with one sentence about why it matters.
  • A thank-you to a colleague or mentor, with their permission.

What to avoid

Avoid complaints about former employers, personal problems or politics unless they are directly relevant. Keep posts positive and professional.

title: LinkedIn etiquette: messages that get replies
excerpt: A well-written message is far more likely to get a response. Here is how to write LinkedIn messages that people want to answer.
content_html:
Recruiters and professionals receive many messages. A short, specific and polite message stands out, while a long or generic one is often ignored.

Good practice

  • Use the person's name and a clear reason for contacting them.
  • Keep the message to three or four sentences.
  • Ask one simple question, or make one clear request.
  • Thank them, whatever the response.

Example

"Hi Niamh, I saw your post about the new warehouse opening in Cork. I have five years' stock control experience and would be interested in learning more about the supervisor role. Would you be open to a short call?"

title: How to attract employers to contact you
excerpt: Being easy to find and clear about what you offer can bring employers to you. Here is how to make that happen.
content_html:
Most job searches involve applying to employers. But some people are approached directly, because their profile matches what a company needs.

Make yourself findable

Use the job titles and skills that employers search for in your headline, About section and skills list. Keep your location and availability visible.

Show your work

Share short examples of what you have done, such as a project summary, a training certificate or a published piece. Concrete evidence is more persuasive than claims.

Stay active

A profile that is updated regularly appears more active. Make small updates each month.

title: Building a personal brand as a jobseeker
excerpt: A personal brand is simply a clear reputation for what you do well. Here is how to build one without pretending to be someone else.
content_html:
Your personal brand is how people describe you when you are not in the room. For jobseekers, it can be a quiet advantage.

Define your focus

Choose two or three things you are known for, such as reliability, customer care or organising events. Use these consistently across your CV, LinkedIn and interviews.

Back it up

Every claim should be supported by evidence, such as an achievement, a reference or a certificate.

Be yourself

Authenticity matters. A brand that reflects your real strengths is easier to sustain than one you invent.

title: Portfolios and online work samples for non-designers
excerpt: A portfolio is not just for designers. Here is how people in other fields can show their work clearly and professionally.
content_html:
A portfolio gives evidence of what you have produced. It can help teachers, administrators, engineers, marketers and many other professionals stand out.

What to include

  • Short case studies: the problem, what you did and the result.
  • Documents you can share, such as reports, presentations or procedures, with names removed where needed.
  • Photos of events or projects you led, with permission.

Protect confidential information

Never share private data, client information or internal documents that you are not allowed to publish. Ask permission, or create a sanitised example.

title: Networking events in Cork: how to get the most from them
excerpt: Networking events can lead to job leads and useful contacts. Here is how to approach them with confidence.
content_html:
Many people dislike networking, but events can be a practical way to meet employers and people in your field. A simple plan makes them less daunting.

Before the event

  • Check who is attending, if the organisers share a list.
  • Prepare your 60-second introduction.
  • Decide on two or three people you would like to meet.

During the event

Ask open questions, listen carefully and be generous with information. People remember those who listened.

After the event

Send a short follow-up message within a few days. Mention where you met and one point from your conversation.

title: Informational interviews: asking for advice, not a job
excerpt: An informational interview is a short conversation to learn about a role or sector. Here is how to ask for one politely.
content_html:
Informational interviews are a low-pressure way to learn from people who work in a field you are interested in. They are not job interviews, and it is important to make that clear.

How to ask

Send a short message: "I am exploring a move into healthcare support and admire your career path. Would you be willing to spend 15 minutes sharing advice on how you got started?"

What to ask

  • What does a typical week look like in this role?
  • What skills matter most, and how did you learn them?
  • What advice would you give someone starting out?

Thank them

Send a thank-you note afterwards. If they offer to keep in touch, do so respectfully.

title: Following up with a recruiter
excerpt: A recruiter may be your route to the next interview. Here is how to follow up without being pushy.
content_html:
Recruiters manage many candidates at once. A polite, well-timed follow-up keeps you in mind without becoming a nuisance.

When to follow up

If the recruiter gave a timeline, wait until the day after it passes. If not, wait about a week after your application or conversation.

What to say

"I wanted to check whether there is any update on the role we discussed. I remain very interested and am happy to provide anything else you need."

Keep it brief

One follow-up is usually enough. If you do not hear back, consider the role closed and move on.

title: Recruitment agencies in Ireland: how they work and how to use them
excerpt: Recruitment agencies can help you find temporary and permanent roles. Here is how they work and how to get the best from them.
content_html:
Recruitment agencies are used by many employers in Ireland, especially for temporary, contract and specialist roles. They are paid by employers, so it is free for you to register.

How to use them well

  • Register with several agencies that cover your sector.
  • Be clear about the roles, hours and locations you want.
  • Keep your CV current, so the consultant can match you quickly.
  • Ask what the employer's process is, and what you can expect next.

Watch for warning signs

Be wary of any agency that asks for payment, bank details or a fee to find you work. Legitimate agencies do not charge jobseekers for registration or placement.

title: Showing your value without bragging
excerpt: Employers want to hear about your achievements, but they also value modesty. Here is how to strike the right balance.
content_html:
Many people struggle to describe their strengths without sounding arrogant. The solution is to focus on facts, outcomes and contributions to others.

Use facts, not adjectives

Say "I reduced complaints by 20% over six months by introducing a short feedback call" rather than "I am an excellent problem solver".

Credit your team

Where a result was shared, say so. "We" is often accurate, and it shows you work well with others.

Be specific about your role

Explain what you personally did. Interviewers want to know your contribution, not just the team's success.

title: Keeping your job search going through a long process
excerpt: Some searches take months. Here is how to stay motivated, organised and realistic over a longer period.
content_html:
A long job search can be draining. Setbacks are normal, and they are easier to manage with a routine and realistic expectations.

Keep a routine

Set regular hours for applications, networking and learning. Take breaks, exercise and spend time on things that are not about work.

Measure effort, not only outcomes

Track the number of applications, conversations and improvements you make. Effort is in your control, even when results are not.

Ask for support

Talk to friends, a careers adviser or a local employment service. Another person's view can help you see opportunities you have missed.
